strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: measuring stereotypical preferences in masked language models and tracking changes after continued pretraining. Token prediction ranks and probability gaps provide an intuitive starting point for this investigation.

The evaluation covers four standard MLMs, CrowS-Pairs and StereoSet, multiple bias categories, and established scoring baselines. Detailed category-level tables and distribution plots make the observed differences inspectable.

Retraining on stereotypical and anti-stereotypical sentences provides a useful sensitivity sanity check. CRR, ΔP, and ΔPA recover the expected direction in all 72 reported model/category/retraining-direction conditions, supporting their ability to detect changes in this experimental setting.
weaknesses: The retraining experiment does not establish the claimed superiority in social-bias measurement accuracy. Section 4.3 describes an 80/20 training/validation split, but the reported bias evaluations appear to use the full CrowS-Pairs dataset, including training examples; no disjoint test results are provided. After 30 epochs, improved reconstruction of these sentences can reflect memorization. The reported 100% accuracy concerns 72 expected condition-level directions, rather than independently established bias judgments. Held-out evaluation and neutral or balanced retraining controls are needed to distinguish bias sensitivity from ordinary learning of the training sentences.

The human-agreement evidence is weak. In Figure 3, the best AUROC is 0.571 versus AUL's 0.569 for BERT, and 0.572 versus 0.566 for RoBERTa. These are small gains with performance close to chance, only 58 negative pairs, and no confidence intervals or paired significance tests. Moreover, the annotations concern whether dataset sentences express stereotypes, not whether a particular model exhibits biased preferences. This provides only indirect validation of the proposed measures.

The interpretation and statistical validation of the change score require correction. If T1 equals T2, Equation 16 returns 0, although scores below 50 are interpreted as a shift toward anti-stereotypical sentences. Tie handling therefore needs explicit treatment, particularly for rank-based measures. Additionally, McNemar's test evaluates changes in binary preference signs, whereas BSRT compares changes in score gaps; its significance marks do not directly validate the reported BSRT statistic. Section 4.2 also infers differences between models from within-model significance tests, which do not establish those between-model differences.

Several substantive interpretations exceed the evidence. An anti-stereotypical sentence is not necessarily biased against an advantaged group: both StereoSet examples in Table 6 concern Ethiopian men, with only the attribute changing. Likewise, disagreement with the proposed metrics does not establish that existing methods underestimate religious or disability bias. These conclusions require an independent reference and clearer separation of stereotypical preference, prediction difficulty, and group-directed social bias.

The contribution of the new components is insufficiently isolated. CRR and the underlying prediction-gap approach build directly on prior work, while the evaluation lacks a standard full-token pseudo-log-likelihood baseline using the same masking procedure. Equation 10 changes the rank transformation from 1−1/r to 1+log(r) while also adding attention weights, so CRR-versus-CRRA comparisons do not isolate attention weighting. Matched baselines and component ablations are needed to explain the reported gains.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the specified checkpoints, masking probability, and epoch count. The manuscript omits optimizer, learning rate, batch size, random seeds, exact partitions, and precise attention aggregation details, and provides no implementation link. Equations 1–2 also sum over all sentence tokens despite the prose describing restricted token sets, leaving baseline implementation uncertain. These specification gaps and the unresolved validation issues prevent a positive Findings recommendation; a next-cycle revision should provide complete protocols and corrected, independent evaluations.
